scenario: AITA for pulling a sickie so I can go to a job interview? | TL;DR at the end I work as a nurse in a community hospital. When I first started working there, I absolutely loved it. However, due to various site closures, we've basically become a 'dumping ground' for patients who can't go home, but can't stay in hospital. I was mostly fine with it, as we were a palliative/end of life (EOL) unit with patients who had complex health issues. Now, we're basically a free care home. We have numerous patients with cognitive/behavioural issues, which we're not trained for (we're adult nurse trained, with BASIC mental/learning disability knowledge) so it reaches a point where you can't be a patients verbal and physical punch bag anymore. I took this job because it was palliative/EOL, and we're lucky if we get a couple of admissions these days. My boss is also awful. She's always been blunt with her staff, which at first I respected, because at least you knew where you stood. Now, she will pick at anything for an excuse to tell at you. Her complaints over the last few months have gotten even more cutting and demoralising; a few prime examples are complaining we don't 'use our initiative' however as soon as we do, she tells us it's wrong. She's accused us of 'killing patients' by not offering our EOL patients food (they're basically comatose, have no swallow, and would likely die from choking rather than their actual condition) and she tried to report me for a drug error that wasn't actually wrong. It wasn't until the medical team AND THE PEOPLE WHO WROTE THE GUIDELINES ON THE Drug told her that I was right, she backed down. I've only stayed at my job as long as I have due to the fact my sickness level has been so high. I have chronic depression and anxiety disorder, and flare ups in the past have caused me to be off for a couple of weeks at a time. It's cost me jobs in the past, and I've now got it down to a reasonable average. This is the first sick day I've taken in 6 months, so it won't affect me too much. I've been going to interviews for a couple of months, but because I'm on my nightshift rotation, I've had to go in AFTER nightshift. Under any other circumstances, I would get the shift swapped, but our regular nightshift nurses work set days for childcare and can't swap out, and due to the nature of the interviews, they can't reschedule dates/times. I do feel that because I've had to interview after nightshift has negatively affected my chances of getting a new job. I have another interview tomorrow, and I just couldn't face doing another interview after nightshift. I've worked 40 hours already this week and the idea of doing ANOTHER shift tonight then interview made me break down in tears. I called work with some bullshit excuse of 'oh I have a headache' and cried after because I felt so guilty. So, Reddit. AITA? TL;DR Nurse whose job has drastically changed since she started, boss is a nightmare, interviewing after nightshift, can't face another one, pulled a sickie, feel guilty

Cash Hongbao (Traditional & Safe)** - **Amount:** Follow local customs (e.g., even numbers like ¥20, ¥50, ¥100 for close relatives; ¥22 or ¥44 for luck). Avoid odd numbers or ¥4 (sounds like "death" in Mandarin). - **Packaging:** - **Red envelopes (红包袋):** Buy pre-made ones at supermarkets (e.g., Walmart, Costco) or online (Taobao, Amazon). Look for **gold/red foil** for extra festivity. - **DIY:** Use red paper (available at craft stores) + glue/stickers. Add a **gold seal (印章)** or calligraphy for a personal touch. - **Alternative:** Use **red envelopes with QR codes** (e.g., WeChat Pay/Alipay) for digital hongbao (if your cousins are tech-savvy). **B. Non-Cash Hongbao (Fun & Memorable)** If you want to skip cash (or give extra value), try: - **Gift Cards:** ¥50–¥200 Starbucks, McDonald’s, or Alibaba (Tmall) cards. Kids love these! - **Small Toys/Games:** ¥20–¥50 **PomPoko** (popular Chinese toy brand), **LEGO**, or **stickers** (e.g., Disney, Hello Kitty). - **Food Coupons:** Vouchers for their favorite snacks (e.g., "¥30 for a box of Mooncakes" or "¥50 for a meal at [local restaurant]"). - **Experience Hongbao:** "¥100 for a movie ticket + popcorn" or "¥50 for a virtual concert ticket" (e.g., Bilibili or Tencent Music). - **Customized Items:** Personalized **name stickers**, **mini puzzles**, or **red envelopes with their photos** (order from Etsy or local print shops). **C. Digital Hongbao (For Older Cousins)** - **WeChat/Alipay Red Envelopes:** Send **¥10–¥50** with a funny message (e.g., "For your future success! 🎉"). Add a **GIF** or **sticker** to make it special. - **Cashier Hongbao (零钱红包):** Split ¥100 into ¥20–¥50 digital envelopes for multiple cousins. --- ### **2. Last-Minute Tips** - **Buy in Bulk:** Supermarkets (e.g., Carrefour, H Mart) or **Taobao** often have red envelopes in packs. Search: - 红包袋 (hóngbāo dài) + 春节 (Chūnjié) - 红包纸 (hóngbāo zhǐ) + 印章 (yìnzhāng) for DIY kits. - **Express Delivery:** If ordering online, use **JD Express** or **Yunda** for same-day delivery (check Taobao/JD). - **Wrap It Nice:** Add a **red ribbon**, **gold washi tape**, or a **handwritten note** (e.g., "祝你新年快乐！" *Zhù nǐ xīnnián kuàilè!* = Happy New Year!). - **Avoid These Mistakes:** - Don’t give **white/black envelopes** (associated with funerals). - Skip **odd amounts** (e.g., ¥15) or ¥4 (bad luck). - Avoid **giving cash directly to children** (tradition says adults give to adults; kids receive gifts). --- ### **3. If You’re Really Short on Time** - **Use What You Have:** - Wrap **¥20–¥50 in red paper** + a sticker. - Give **a small toy + ¥10** (e.g., a keychain + cash). - **Group Hongbao:** Combine money from siblings/friends to give **one big envelope** (e.g., ¥200 total split among cousins). - **Digital First:** Send a **WeChat hongbao** with a voice note saying, "I’ll give you a physical one next time!" --- ### **4. Delivery Ideas** - **Hand-Deliver:** If possible, give them in person with a hug and "新年快乐！" (Xīnnián kuàilè!). - **Post It:** Use **China Post** (if they’re far) or **JD Courier** (fast and reliable). - **Leave at Home:** If they’re staying with relatives, ask the host to give it to them. --- ### **5. Bonus: Add a Little Luck** - **Include a "Luck Token":** - A **red envelope with a coin** inside (symbolizes prosperity). - A **small "福" (fú = luck) charm** or **mandarin orange** (symbolizes wealth). - A **handwritten fortune** (e.g., "This year, you’ll get an A+ in exams!"). --- ### **Example Checklist (1-Hour Prep)** | Task | Where to Get It | Cost (Approx.) | |--------------------|--------------------------|----------------| | Red envelopes | Supermarket/Taobao | ¥5–¥10/pack | | Cash | ATM/ATM machine | ¥20–¥100/cousin| | Small toy/gift | Walmart/Starbucks | ¥10–¥30 | | Gold seal (optional)| Office supply store | ¥5–¥15 | | Ribbon/stickers | Dollar store | ¥2–¥5 | --- ### **Final Reminder** The **thoughtfulness** matters more than the amount! Even a **handmade envelope with ¥20 and a smile** will make them happy. If you’re still unsure, **digital hongbao** is the safest bet. **祝你包红包顺利！** (Zhù nǐ bāo hóngbāo shùnlì! = Wish you smooth hongbao-giving!) Burnout is a **public health crisis**, and taking time off when needed is **not laziness**—it’s **self-preservation**. - **The guilt is misplaced.** - You’re feeling guilty because you **internalized the toxic culture** ("I should just suck it up"). But: - **You’re not "abandoning" patients.** You’re **protecting yourself** so you can return when you’re functional. A burned-out nurse is **less safe** for patients than a well-rested one. - **Your employer benefits from your absence.** If you’re constantly exhausted, your performance suffers, and patients (and your colleagues) suffer. A sick day is **not a failure**—it’s a **necessary reset**. --- ### **2. Is It "Right" to Pull a Sickie?** **Yes, if:** - You **genuinely need the time off** (and your health is declining). - You’ve **exhausted all other options** (e.g., talking to HR, requesting a transfer, or discussing workload adjustments). - You’re **honest with yourself** about why you’re taking the day (even if you lie to your boss, you know the truth). - You **plan to return** when you’re better (not using it as an excuse to quit without notice). **No, if:** - You’re **using it as a permanent escape** (e.g., you’re already mentally checked out and just want to avoid work). - You **don’t have a backup plan** (e.g., no interviews lined up, no savings, no other income). - You’re **exploiting the system** (e.g., taking frequent sick days without addressing the root issues). --- ### **3. The Broader Picture: Is Your Job "Wrong"?** Your situation raises **systemic issues** in healthcare: - **Palliative care is being diluted.** Hospitals are **offloading responsibility** onto understaffed, undertrained teams. This is **not sustainable** and puts **undue stress on nurses**. - **Mental health support is lacking.** If your employer **doesn’t address burnout**, they’re **failing their staff**—and ultimately, their patients. - **Toxic leadership is rampant.** A boss who **blames staff for systemic failures** is **not a leader**—they’re a **liability**. **What you could do instead of a sickie:** 1. **Document everything.** Keep records of: - Your boss’s unfair criticisms. - The shift in your role (e.g., emails about "care-home" patients). - Any mental health flare-ups (if you can, get notes from a doctor). - This could help if you **leave abruptly** or **file a complaint**. 2. **Talk to HR (if you dare).** Frame it as: > *"I’m struggling with my workload and mental health. I need support to either transfer to a palliative unit or discuss adjustments."* (But be prepared for **gaslighting**—your boss might dismiss you.) 3. **Start job hunting aggressively.** If you’re interviewing, **prioritize roles with:** - Clear palliative/EOL focus. - **Mental health support** for staff. - **Fair leadership** (check Glassdoor reviews). 4. **Consider resignation with notice.** If you’re **done**, give **2–4 weeks’ notice** (if possible) to avoid burning bridges. Frame it as: > *"I’ve decided to pursue a role that better aligns with my skills and well-being."* --- ### **4. The Interview After Nightshift Issue** This is **a separate ethical dilemma**: - **Is it fair to expect you to perform at 100% after a 12-hour shift?** - **No.** Your body and mind are **not machines**.
